items.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
items.abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
items.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED APPROACHES TO FORECASTING AND OPTIMIZATION OF COMPLEX SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Forecasting and optimization form an integrated foundation for the intelligent management of complex systems in industry, logistics, energy, transportation, and service operations. The interaction of multiple components, changing operating conditions, and interconnected decisions creates valuable opportunities for data-driven modeling and adaptive resource allocation. This study presents a comparative literature-based analysis of statistical forecasting, machine learning, deep learning, mathematical optimization, and reinforcement learning approaches. Their suitability is examined in relation to temporal patterns, explanatory variables, uncertainty representation, computational requirements, and decision objectives. Particular attention is given to hybrid architectures that connect probabilistic forecasts with optimization models and continuously updated decisions. The synthesis establishes a conceptual framework for evaluating forecasting quality alongside operational performance and identifies promising directions for intelligent management of dynamic complex systems.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of conventional nursing versus data-driven predictive nursing models in orthopedic trauma patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Orthopedic injuries have necessitated the adoption of appropriate nursing interventions to promote favorable healing and minimize risks and complications associated with these conditions. In recent times, predictive nursing models that use artificial intelligence have generated considerable interest, particularly for comparison with traditional nursing interventions. To determine the comparative effectiveness of traditional nursing interventions versus data-driven predictive nursing models in orthopedic injury cases. A systematic review of 33 studies, including randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, quasi-experiments, and machine-learning-based prediction studies, was conducted. Pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were computed by employing a random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis approach. Heterogeneity between studies was measured with I-squared statistics, while publication bias was detected with Egger’s test and funnel plot analyses. There was a statistically significant improvement in all intervention categories compared to the control group. Traditional and perioperative nursing interventions had an overall OR of 2.13 (95% CI 1.74–2.61), whereas postoperative rehabilitation interventions had an OR of 1.97 (95% CI 1.37–2.84). The machine learning-based predictive models had an OR of 2.26 (1.89–2.71), whereas the predictive nursing decision-support systems had an OR of 2.14 (1.70–2.68). Prognostic studies also had OR 2.27 (1.82–2.83). The heterogeneity was at most moderate, and there was no publication bias except in prognostic studies. Predictive and conventional nursing strategies both significantly improve orthopedic trauma outcomes, with predictive models offering greater potential for individualized care.

items.title: Complementary Error Profiles of Human Readers and Large Language Models in Detecting AI-Generated Chest Radiographs: A Comparative Reader Study
items.abstract: Abstract Frontier large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models can generate realistic chest radiographs, raising concerns for dataset integrity when provenance metadata are absent. We compared authenticity judgments by two radiologists, two nonradiologist physicians, and three frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8) on 160 posteroanterior radiographs: 40 real NIH ChestX-ray14 images and 120 synthetic images generated from text by three pipelines. Each evaluator judged every image once; the LLM evaluation was repeated twice 3 months later. Balanced accuracy was the primary metric, given 75% synthetic prevalence. The two best evaluators reached nearly identical balanced accuracy from opposite operating points: Gemini 3.5 Flash had the highest point estimate (77.9%; specificity 100%, sensitivity 55.8%) and RAD1 was a close second (75.8%; specificity 55.0%, sensitivity 96.7%), a paired difference of − 2.1 percentage points (95% CI, − 5.8 to 1.2). On repetition, LLM judgments were not fully reproducible and this ordering did not hold. Nonradiologists performed near chance. All four human readers detected diffusion-generated images at 82–100%, whereas the radiologists misclassified 38–45% of real images and the conservative LLMs reached perfect specificity yet detected only 32–72% of LLM-generated images. With laterality markers and borders masked, specificity was 62.5% (Gemini) and 85.0% (GPT-5.5) against 90–100% in same-day unmasked runs. Interevaluator agreement was low throughout (Fleiss’ kappa among LLMs 0.213). A frequency-domain baseline reached 98.3% balanced accuracy within this dataset but 12% sensitivity on a held-out generator. Human readers and LLMs failed on different images; visual authenticity assessment alone may be insufficient for provenance verification.

items.title: Computational approaches to deep learning–driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

items.title: Construction and content validation of an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching framework for the liquor factory design course in local undergraduate universities: a modified Delphi study
items.abstract: The digital, intelligent and green transformation of the Chinese baijiu industry has introduced new competency demands for liquor engineering education. The Liquor Factory Design course is a comprehensive upper-level engineering design course for students in the liquor engineering program that combines knowledge of brewing technology, chemical engineering, engineering drawing, brewing equipment, energy-saving and environmental protection, and production management. However, the course in local undergraduate universities still has several problems, such as an unclear design task chain, a lack of authentic engineering contexts, ambiguous boundaries for the use of artificial intelligence, and an assessment approach that focuses too much on the final product rather than the learning process. The above problems may limit the all-round development of students’ engineering design abilities. Given the above problems, this paper builds an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching system for the Liquor Factory Design course by integrating Outcome-Based Education, Artificial Intelligence and Complex Engineering Design. A modified Delphi method was employed to examine the content validity and refine the framework. Two rounds of expert consultations were conducted with university teachers, engineering technicians from Baijiu Enterprise, and experts from an engineering design institution. The first round of results showed that, although most experts agreed that a framework was needed, they raised concerns about the limits of AI application, the viability of sustained cooperation between enterprises and mentors, a lack of genuine engineering resources, and an unfinished chain of evaluation evidence. Based on expert feedback, AI was repositioned as a tool for learning support and design reasoning rather than automatic design generation. A complex engineering design task chain was established, including production scale determination, process flow design, material balance, equipment selection, workshop layout, energy conservation and environmental protection, drawing expression, and design defense. In addition, industrial case libraries, equipment parameter databases, engineering drawing resources, and an evidence-based assessment mechanism were incorporated into the framework. The second-round results showed increased mean scores, reduced coefficients of variation, and greater concordance among participating experts. These results reflect expert consensus on the revised framework, while student learning effectiveness was not evaluated in this study. The proposed framework may support the transformation of the Liquor Factory Design course from a report-oriented model to a competence-oriented model and provide a reference for cultivating complex engineering design competence in liquor engineering programs in local undergraduate universities in China.

items.title: Consumer Behavioural Insights for AI-Enabled Personalized Food Waste Reduction in Restaurants
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly enabling restaurants to deliver personalized customer experiences while supporting sustainable business practices. However, the effectiveness of AI-enabled interventions depends on understanding the behavioural factors that influence consumer food waste. This study examines consumer behaviour related to restaurant food waste and explores how behavioural insights can inform AI-driven personalization strategies for food waste reduction. The research is grounded in the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) and is based on primary data collected from 100 restaurant consumers in the Mumbai Suburban region using a structured questionnaire. The study assessed six behavioural constructs: awareness, attitude, behavioural factors, psychological factors, social factors, and willingness to act towards food waste reduction. Descriptive analysis revealed that respondents demonstrated relatively high levels of awareness (Mean = 3.89) and positive attitudes (Mean = 3.92) towards reducing food waste. Psychological factors (Mean = 3.81) and social factors (Mean = 3.64) also indicated favourable behavioural orientations. However, behavioural practices recorded comparatively lower scores (Mean = 3.45), suggesting an attitude–behaviour gap in responsible food consumption. Respondents also expressed a positive willingness to adopt food waste reduction practices (Mean = 3.76), indicating the potential for targeted behavioural interventions. Based on these findings, the study proposes an AI-driven consumer insight framework that can support restaurants in designing personalized food waste reduction strategies, including portion-size recommendations, smart menu suggestions, and digital nudges. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for managerial decision-making, the framework demonstrates how consumer behavioural data can be leveraged to enhance AI-enabled customer engagement and sustainability initiatives. The study contributes to the growing discourse on AI in Business and Marketing by illustrating the role of behavioural insights in developing customer-centric and sustainable restaurant practices. The findings offer practical implications for restaurant managers seeking to integrate AI-enabled personalization with food waste reduction initiatives in the HORECA sector. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Consumer Behaviour, Food Waste, Restaurant Management, Theory of Planned Behaviour, Sustainability, HORECA.

items.title: Consumer Decision-Making in Digital Commerce: Effects of Virtual Influencer Motive Attributions on Trust, Perceived Risk, and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In AI-enabled digital commerce, consumers evaluate virtual influencers (VIs) not only through source characteristics but also by inferring why they create content and recommend products. This study examines how perceived intrinsic and commercially oriented extrinsic motives are associated with trust, perceived risk, and purchase intention. Survey data from 295 South Korean consumers aged 20–39 were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 23.0 for descriptive and reliability analyses and IBM SPSS Amos 24.0 for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Perceived intrinsic motivation was positively associated with trust but was not significantly associated with perceived risk or directly with purchase intention. Perceived extrinsic motivation was negatively associated with trust and purchase intention and positively associated with perceived risk. Trust was positively associated with purchase intention, whereas the conditional association of perceived risk was nonsignificant. Supplementary bootstrap analyses supported specific indirect associations through trust for both motive attributions, consistent with full (indirect-only) mediation for intrinsic motivation and partial mediation for extrinsic motivation within the specified model. Neither specific indirect association through perceived risk was significant. These findings distinguish consumers’ confidence in a recommending persona from their uncertainty about a recommended purchase and identify trust as a central statistical mediator of motive attribution and purchase intention in VI marketing.

items.title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

items.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
items.abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

items.title: Cough Sounds for the Recognition of Multiclass Respiratory Diseases With Artificial Intelligence: A Review
items.abstract: Respiratory diseases such as asthma, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis, and COVID-19 require timely recognition and appropriate medical evaluation. Cough is a common symptom of many respiratory conditions and contains acoustic characteristics that can provide useful information for disease recognition. This report presents a review of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for recognizing multiclass respiratory diseases using cough sounds. The review examines cough datasets, audio preprocessing, feature extraction, and Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques used for cough analysis. Common methods include noise reduction, cough segmentation, Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), Mel-spectrograms, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The review also discusses applications, advantages, limitations, and evaluation methods. Findings indicate that AI-based cough analysis has potential as a non-invasive and accessible supportive screening technology. However, challenges such as limited datasets, background noise, class imbalance, recording-device variations, similar acoustic patterns, model generalization, privacy, and clinical validation remain. Future research should focus on larger and diverse datasets, explainable AI, smartphone-based systems, multimodal analysis, and clinical validation for reliable respiratory disease recognition.

items.title: Creating Digital Public Value in Platform States
items.abstract: As states adopt platform-based models of public governance, understanding how institutional capabilities and governance arrangements translate into societal value has become a central concern for public administration research. No quantitative model had jointly tested how public digital capability, data governance, and platform governance interact to shape digital platform use and digital public value creation in emerging economies such as Morocco. This chapter develops and empirically validates an integrative tripartite structural model grounded in Public Value Theory, New Public Management, and Sociotechnical Theory, using PLS-SEM on a sample of 350 Moroccan public employees, civil servants, and citizens. All seven hypotheses were confirmed at p < 0.001: public digital capability and platform governance emerged as the strongest direct determinants of platform use, which fully mediates digital public value creation. The chapter offers theoretical and managerial insights for decision-makers engaged in digital transformation in emerging platform states.

items.title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE FEASIBILITY OF USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS THROUGH THE LENS OF THE BRAZILIAN SOCIETY OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES GUIDELINES FOR ANTIMICROBIAL STEWARDSHIP IN GRAM-NEGATIVE BACTERIAL INFECTIONS
items.abstract: The global emergence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacilli represents one of the major global public health challenges today, requiring structured interventions for antimicrobial stewardship. The guidelines of the Brazilian Society of Infectious Diseases (SBI) establish rigorous, evidence-based therapeutic protocols for the treatment of severe infections caused by carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii. The SBI emphasizes the selection of initial empirical coverage grounded in local epidemiology and microbiological profiles, the optimization of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, as well as mandatory reassessment at 48 to 72 hours to promote early therapeutic de-escalation. This article presents an expanded narrative and critical-analytical review on the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a clinical decision support tool to enable and operationalize the implementation of SBI guidelines at the hospital bedside. The study delves into the main applications of AI, including individualized prediction of resistance risk upon admission, accelerated predictive antibiograms via mass spectrometry and deep learning, real-time precision dosing, and natural language processing for auditing narrative records in electronic health records, critically contrasting them with the reasons justifying the absence of AI in official protocols of other international medical organizations and the SBI itself. From the perspective of Brazilian regulation, the study analyzes in detail compliance with the General Data Protection Law (LGPD) and Resolution CFM No. 2,454/2026 of the Federal Council of Medicine, which categorically prohibits prescriptive autonomy for automated systems, ensuring the centrality of medical judgment and enshrining the 'human-in-the-loop' paradigm.

items.title: Cybercrime in India under the New Criminal Laws: Emerging Challenges in Investigation, Digital Evidence and Criminal Justice
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital technology has changed the way people communicate, conduct business, access financial services and interact with government institutions. At the same time, this transformation has created new opportunities for criminal activity. Cybercrime today includes online financial fraud, identity theft, unauthorised access to computer systems, cyberstalking, impersonation, data theft, social media offences and technologically facilitated forms of traditional crime. The investigation and prosecution of such offences present difficulties that differ from those associated with conventional crimes because electronic evidence can be easily altered, deleted, transferred and stored across multiple jurisdictions. The introduction of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 represents a significant transformation of India's criminal justice framework. This paper examines the implications of the new criminal laws for cybercrime investigation, digital evidence and criminal justice administration. It also considers the continuing importance of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the constitutional protection of privacy and due process. The paper adopts a doctrinal and analytical methodology based on legislation, judicial decisions and authoritative legal materials. It argues that legislative reform by itself cannot adequately address the complexity of cybercrime. Effective enforcement requires trained investigators, modern forensic infrastructure, rapid preservation of electronic evidence, coordination between investigative agencies and service providers, and appropriate safeguards for individual rights. The paper further examines emerging challenges associated with artificial intelligence, deepfakes, digital impersonation and sophisticated online fraud. It concludes that India's new criminal laws provide an important foundation for dealing with cybercrime, but their success will ultimately depend upon effective implementation, technological capacity and a careful balance between criminal enforcement and constitutional liberties.

items.title: Data Analytics and AI
items.abstract: Data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming geotechnical monitoring by extracting insights from large sensor datasets. This chapter covers analytics objectives (trend detection, anomaly identification, and prediction) and data types (time-series, spatial, imagery, and point clouds). We discuss preprocessing: cleaning, labeling, and metadata standards. Exploratory analysis and visualization techniques are highlighted. Statistical methods (trend tests, change-point detection) and uncertainty quantification are reviewed. Time-series tools include filtering, smoothing, ARIMA, and Kalman filters (with equations). We survey anomaly detection approaches: simple thresholds, statistical tests, and unsupervised ML (clustering, PCA/autoencoders). Supervised learning for classification/regression (feature selection, model validation, and metrics like ROC/AUC) is covered. Deep learning methods (LSTMs/RNNs for sequences, CNNs/Transformers for images, PointNets for clouds) and physics-informed neural networks are introduced. Digital twins and the integration of ML with geomechanical models are discussed. Real-time analytics, streaming, and edge inference (MLOps) are addressed, as are alarm logic, false-positive management, and human-in-the-loop frameworks. We emphasize explainability, model validation, and regulatory guidance. Two worked examples illustrate a Kalman filter update and an ROC curve calculation. Tables compare algorithms (data needs, latency, interpretability), and a mermaid diagram shows an analytics pipeline. Case studies (slope failure warning, tailings instability, digital twin of a mine) demonstrate real-world AI use. Checklists (data preparation, model deployment) and a full References section are provided. AI’s promise in geotechnics is “step-change” improvements in efficiency and safety.

items.title: Data Analytics and Big Data in Cybersecurity Threat Detection: A Critical Review of Techniques, Challenges, and Emerging Directions
items.abstract: The increasing sophistication and scale of cyber threats have intensified the need for analytical methods capable of processing high-volume, high-velocity, and heterogeneous security data. This critical review synthesizes 38 scholarly sources identified through a structured Google Scholar search and a PRISMA-informed screening workflow to examine the role of data analytics and big data in cybersecurity threat detection. The review considers signature-based, anomaly-based, behaviour-based, machine-learning, and deep-learning approaches, together with operational challenges and emerging directions. Across heterogeneous datasets and application settings, machine-learning and deep-learning methods offer strong representation-learning and pattern-recognition capabilities, while anomaly- and behaviour-based approaches remain important for identifying previously unseen or context-dependent activity. Their practical effectiveness, however, depends on data quality, labelling, class balance, computational resources, interpretability, privacy, and the operating environment. Because the underlying studies use different datasets, tasks, metrics, and validation designs, the evidence does not support a universal ranking of detection approaches. Current research increasingly emphasises explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning, privacy-preserving analytics, hybrid detection architectures, and real-time processing. The review concludes that robust cybersecurity analytics requires context-appropriate combinations of complementary techniques rather than reliance on a single universally superior model.

items.title: Decomposing and Predicting Annotation Disagreement in Harmful Content Across Languages
items.abstract: Annotator disagreement is increasingly recognized as a meaningful property of subjective tasks, rather than merely noise to be removed. Predicting which items are likely to be contested could help allocate annotation effort and route difficult cases to human review. We propose predicting disagreement from interpretable semantic properties of the text. An LLM answers a set of binary questions covering harmful-content characteristics, disagreement-related cues such as borderline severity and missing context, and language-sensitive cues such as local slurs. A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.

items.title: Deconstructing the Menstrual Barrier to Education: Examining Psychological, Social, and Structural Barriers in the Somali Region of Ethiopia
items.abstract: Documentation detailing the relative inaccessibility of education in Ethiopia’s Somali Region continues to grow. Structural barriers—including limited access to school programs, a shortage of qualified teachers, insufficient funding, and scarce learning resources—act as compounding disadvantages for all learners. These realities are further exacerbated for adolescent girls by inadequate access to dedicated gender-responsive washrooms (private latrines and clean water) essential for Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM). When girls lack access to private, gender responsive facilities, physical limitations become a catalyst for acute psychological distress. This psychological distress (marked by shame and embarrassment), combined with social pressures (leading to planned absenteeism) and diminished cognitive engagement (distraction caused by the ongoing anxiety of leakage), results in lower overall attendance and academic achievement. These factors define the parameters of social disapproval surrounding female education. The social disapproval associated with menstruation directly impacts girls' intentions to attend school while menstruating, acting as a socially constructed mechanism of exclusion that violates the fundamental right to education enshrined by UNESCO. This study (n=450) compares girls with access to re-useable MHM kits, paired with health education to a control group. This represents a baseline study to then revisit longitudinally to see if having access to reliable MHM changes beliefs and behaviours around school attendance and engagement during menstruation. A theory-driven principal component analysis explored key factors influencing school attendance and engagement for girls in the Somali Region of Ethiopia.

items.title: Deepfakes and bots in digital disinformation driven by malicious artificial intelligence
items.abstract: In an increasingly uncertain digital environment, how do we know if what we see is real? Deepfakes, which include videos with fake faces, synthetic audio, and manipulated documents, along with social bots that interact and persuade as if they were humans, represent a growing threat driven by malicious artificial intelligence. These technologies not only spread disinformation but also generate collective emotions such as fear, indignation, and distrust, affecting democratic stability and social cohesion. Faced with this reality, this article develops a bibliometric study and a scoping review of the literature (2014-2024) based on 316 documents indexed in Scopus, with the purpose of identifying trends, influential authors, methodological approaches, and research gaps on the use of artificial intelligence in disinformation. The results show an annual growth of 97%, an average age of 2.2 years per document, 19.7 average citations, and an h-index of 37, evidencing the sustained expansion and scientific interest in the detection of deepfakes and bots as central challenges of the digital ecosystem. Production is concentrated in India, the United States, and China. The co-occurrence analysis confirms the main research axes in deepfake detection, deep learning, and CNNs, along with the growing prominence of synthetic speech, diffusion models, and the economic and social effects of social media. Future research should address the role of AI in political communication, in particular its links to disinformation, polarization, and emotional influence, as well as the impact of the EU AI Act, the need for standardised metrics, and the emergence of transnational frameworks for digital governance.

items.title: Deliberation Within AI: A Reproducible Pipeline for Multi-Agent Deliberation Simulation
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have renewed interest in whether large language models can simulate aspects of public deliberation. Current deliberation simulations remain methodologically fragile: fluent conversational outputs are often treated as evidence of deliberative quality despite limited reproducibility, weak safeguards for viewpoint diversity, and limited systematic evaluation. This article argues that AI-deliberation simulations can function as credible analytical instruments only if they incorporate infrastructures for reproducibility, plurality preservation, and deliberative quality assessment. The article develops a stage-structured method for deliberative simulation combining persona validation, plurality auditing, and discourse-quality assessment within a reproducible pipeline. The framework is presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and evaluated through a simulation study on the June 2023 Swiss federal referendum on the Climate and Innovation Act together with a batch replication study comparing direct and structured deliberation architectures. The findings show that, as an integrated theory-driven architecture, the structured pipeline generates more stable deliberative dynamics than unconstrained interaction, including clearer plurality preservation and more coherent opinion updating. At the same time, the simulations remain below human minipublics in terms of contextual grounding and justificatory depth. The article positions AI-deliberation simulations as methodological infrastructures for cumulative and empirically testable research on AI-supported deliberation in digital governance.

items.title: Dependency Restructuring: How Technological Enactment Changes Organizational Requirement Relations
items.abstract: Digital technologies can change organizational work without changing the dependencies through which work is coordinated. This article examines the cases in which those dependencies do change. The analysis separates changes in activities from changes in dependencies and from the coordination needed to manage them. Its main contribution is a bounded meso-level framework that treats dependency restructuring as an independently observable change between technological enactment and subsequent coordination requirements. The framework specifies observable forms of dependency change and derives two conditional propositions. Individual dependency relations may be created, eliminated, or redirected to a different provider; previously separate sets of dependencies may also become connected. The first proposition concerns situations in which local autonomy increases while reliance on a shared technological or external capability also increases. The second concerns situations in which different technologies produce similar coordination requirements because they generate similar dependency configurations under similar organizational conditions. Two evidence-based illustrations—enterprise cloud migration and artificial intelligence integration in organizational workflows—show how the approach can be applied without treating the cases as tests of the theory. The article also provides an empirical identification procedure for distinguishing activity change, dependency change, and coordination response.

items.title: Desafíos y retos en la Encíclica Magnifica Humanitas
items.abstract: The encyclical Magnifica Humanitas of H. H. León XIV reflects on the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to human dignity, emphasizing that technological progress acquires meaning only when it serves the human person and the common good. The document warns about the risks of the technocratic paradigm, the dehumanization of relationships, information manipulation, educational inequalities, and the impact of automation on work. It also proposes a culture of love, solidarity, and justice as the foundation for guiding scientific and technological development. From the perspective of Christian humanism, it highlights the need for an integral education that fosters critical thinking, ethical discernment, and the responsible use of new technologies. Finally, it argues that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, moral responsibility, freedom, and the transcendent vocation of the human person, thereby promoting an authentically human and inclusive form of development.

items.title: Design and Preliminary Evaluation of an Explainable Knowledge-Based Adaptive Cybersecurity Training System in the NIS2 Context
items.abstract: The paper presents the design, implementation, and preliminary evaluation of AICyberTrainer, an explainable knowledge-based adaptive system for personalized employee cybersecurity training. The need for its development emerged from a cybersecurity assessment of six public institutions and public enterprises, which revealed low implementation of security measures, particularly in supply chain security, human factors, and training. The system supports the implementation and monitoring of training measures associated with Article 21(2)(g) of the NIS2 Directive. Personalization is based on the user's job role, organizational context, and identified competency gaps, while training is delivered through serious-game scenarios and transparent inference rules. The evaluation included an initial knowledge assessment of 24 employees and an analysis of the latest assessment attempt for each of 21 unique user codes in the application. The mean initial assessment score was 50.83%, whereas the mean score on the most recent attempts was 80.68%. Sixteen users achieved the threshold of at least 70%. The mean satisfaction rating was 4.78/5, based on 11 responses. The instruments were not calibrated, and records were unpaired, so the group difference cannot establish a training effect. All five users below the threshold were satisfaction non-respondents. The contribution of this study lies in integrating organizational assessment, user modeling, personalized scenarios, and explainable inference into a closed adaptive loop. The system supports training related to NIS2 requirements but does not assess an organization's full legal compliance. items.title: Design Implications for Teacher-Configurable Generative AI Writing Tools: A Participatory Design Study with StoryBot
items.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools become accessible, their integration into K–12 writing presents opportunities and challenges. This study partnered with 21 primary school teachers in a participatory co-design process to develop StoryBot, a teacher-configurable GenAI story-authoring platform. Teachers identified instructional needs and learning outcomes that informed system features, including genre-specific writing scaffolds, configurable prompts, and constraints on full-text generation to preserve student voice. The platform positions educators as co-designers of AI behavior rather than passive users. We conducted a pilot writing workshop with 13 youth (ages 8–12) and a focus group with six educators to examine how the platform influenced students’ writing behaviors and classroom integration. Findings demonstrate the value of teacher co-design and configurable AI systems in aligning GenAI tools with pedagogical priorities and practices. We present design implications for teacher-configurable GenAI writing systems that support student agency, ethical safeguards, and instructional alignment in human–AI coauthoring environments.

items.title: Design of AI-Based Perception Systems for Real-Time ADAS
items.abstract: This chapter examines Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based embedded perception for real-time Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) for trustworthy electric ride-hailing services. It reviews recent perception approaches for road-scene understanding, including lightweight convolutional models, You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors, compact vision transformers, low-light perception, radar-aware methods, and multimodal fusion. Particular attention is given to safety-critical road elements such as pedestrians, vehicles, cyclists, obstacles, traffic signs, and traffic lights, because they directly influence driver awareness, decision-making, and perceived safety. The chapter proposes a methodological framework covering dataset selection, ADAS task definition, data preparation, model selection, AI optimization methods, embedded deployment, and evaluation. By linking perception reliability with perceived safety, user trust, and behavioral intention, the chapter positions embedded ADAS perception as a key contributor to the adoption of electric ride-hailing services.

items.title: Developing and evaluating a remote, self-administered, AI-powered occupational therapy initial assessment: A crossover randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is spreading through health care, yet systems that administer assessments directly to clients remain untested in occupational therapy (OT), where the initial assessment both gathers data and builds therapeutic rapport. Objective To compare user experience of a purpose-built, remote AI-administered OT initial assessment with a human-administered assessment. Methods Thirty adults completed an AI-administered and a human-administered OT initial assessment in randomized order one to two weeks apart (crossover design), rating usability, perceived compassion, goal setting and satisfaction after each and stating an overall preference; 28 gave reflection interviews. Formats were compared within participants (Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar, Holm-corrected) and interviews analyzed thematically. Results Participants were randomized 15 per sequence; order affected no outcome. AI usability was high (modified System Usability Scale 81.1). Perceived compassion favored the human format (median 9.90 vs 7.53; Hodges–Lehmann difference 2.39, 95% CI 1.56–3.11; p < 0.001), as did satisfaction (all p < 0.001). Agreement that goals were clear, personalized, relevant, attainable and motivating did not differ (all p ≥ 0.25), but strong agreement was more frequent after the human format on four of five items (40.0–53.3 percentage points, all p ≤ 0.002). Overall, 83% (25/30) preferred the human format. Four themes were identified. Conclusions The AI-administered assessment was highly usable and produced goals accepted as clear, relevant and attainable at rates matching the human format; what differed was the depth of endorsement, perceived compassion and preference. Conversational AI appears better placed to supplement therapist-led assessment than to replace it.

items.title: DEVELOPING SOCIOLINGUISTIC THINKING IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PEDAGOGICAL PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new participant in everyday and educational communication. Learners now talk to chatbots, use machine translation and receive automated feedback on their writing. This conceptual paper examines how these tools affect the development of sociolinguistic thinking, understood as the ability to select, interpret and adapt language forms according to social context, participants and communicative goals. Drawing on sociocultural theory, social learning theory, sociolinguistics and intercultural pedagogy, the paper outlines the cognitive, social and emotional mechanisms involved and analyzes the opportunities and risks of AI as a language model and interlocutor. It then proposes five pedagogical conditions for developing sociolinguistic thinking in AI-supported learning environments: critical AI literacy, contextualized task design, teacher mediation, comparison of human and machine language, and a supportive psychological climate.

items.title: Development of an artificial intelligence-based automatic plastic waste sorting system
items.abstract: This study describes the development and realization of an intelligent plastic waste sorting system that combines computer vision, robotic control, and a graphical user interface (GUI) for real-time monitoring. The system integrates the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) deep learning architecture to detect and classify seven distinct plastic types: polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), single-use plastics, single-layer plastics, multi-layer plastics, squeeze tubes, and ultra-high-temperature (UHT) boxes. Sorting actions are executed by an EEZYbotARM Mk2 robotic arm, driven by an STM32F446RE microcontroller, which performs autonomous pick-and-place operations according to the recognition output. A custom interface built with Python Qt version 5 (PyQt5) enables live video visualization, delineation of detection areas, counting of identified categories, and additional functionalities such as counter reset, selective filtering, and exporting detection records to Excel. The complete setup was tested on a conveyor-based system, confirming high detection precision, dependable robotic operation, and a user-friendly supervision interface. The trained YOLOv8 model achieves a precision of 94%, recall of 95%, and mean average precision (mAP) at Intersection over Union (IoU) thresholds 0.5–0.95 of 94% across the seven plastic waste categories, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed detection pipeline. This contribution aims to mitigate the limited advancement of plastic recycling technologies in developing regions, offering a cost-effective and practical framework for enhancing plastic waste management.

items.title: Development of EDP.AI: An AI-integrated engineering design module to enhance student engagement in STEM learning
items.abstract: STEM education is a national priority in Malaysia; however, clear gaps in learning outcomes and student participation remain, particularly in rural areas. In Sabah, very low Indeks STEM Murid (ISM) scores, coupled with declining enrolment in the STEM Package A stream, indicate persistent challenges in the quality and continuity of STEM learning at the lower secondary level. These trends suggest that many students do not experience STEM learning as sufficiently meaningful or structured to build confidence and sustain their interest in STEM pathways. This paper reports Phase 1A of a Design and Development Research (DDR) study, focusing on the needs analysis and conceptualisation of EDP.AI, an AI-assisted module designed to scaffold the Engineering Design Process (EDP) for lower secondary students in rural Sabah. Document analysis was conducted to examine challenges related to STEM learning, EDP implementation, artificial intelligence in education, and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) in low-resource contexts. The evidence was synthesised using design rationale mapping to translate theoretical and contextual insights into actionable design decisions. items.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
items.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

items.title: Digital collectives in precarious work: comparing gig workers’ common voices across online communities
items.abstract: As gig workers receive inadequate support from digital labor platforms and (inter)national institutions, many face systemic challenges—such as income insecurity, algorithmic management, and social isolation—and turn to online communities instead. Identification with such shared spaces is fundamental to fostering relational connections and collective practices that help workers cope and succeed. However, these spaces remain poorly understood. This study examines how social media affordances and gig work type shape what social identity scholars call a “common voice” (i.e., the collective expression of identification in an online community). Using computational sentiment analysis and quantitative content analysis of 8,319 posts and 153,440 comments from six of the largest Reddit communities for gig workers, the study finds that common voices emerge, despite the atomizing characteristics of gig work (e.g., geographic dispersion and platform mediation) and the constraint of social cues on the platform that hosts the community. Moreover, common voices significantly differ between platform-specific communities and generic communities for gig workers in themes, sentiments, message length and image use. These findings extend scholarship on gig work, identification, and social media affordances by highlighting their intersection—showing how gig worker communities can act as digital collectives that foster identification and work relationships.

items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies, including the internet, social media, e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, and artificial intelligence-based applications, has fundamentally transformed consumer behavior in the digital marketplace. Consumers are no longer passive recipients of marketing messages; instead, they actively seek information, evaluate alternatives, engage with brands, and make purchasing decisions through various digital channels. This transformation has led to the emergence of Digital Consumer Behavior as a critical determinant of marketing effectiveness and business sustainability in the digital economy. This study aims to examine the influence of Digital Consumer Behavior on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision, as well as to investigate the mediating role of Consumer Trust in this relationship. A quantitative research approach was employed using a survey method involving 100 active digital platform users who had conducted online purchases within the previous six months. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling, and data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The empirical findings reveal that Digital Consumer Behavior has a positive and significant effect on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision. Furthermore, Consumer Trust significantly influences Purchase Decision. The mediation analysis demonstrates that Consumer Trust significantly mediates the relationship between Digital Consumer Behavior and Purchase Decision. The coefficient of determination indicates that the model explains of the variance in Consumer Trust of the variance in Purchase Decision having a strong relationship. These findings provide theoretical support for the integration of digital consumer behavior and consumer trust perspectives within contemporary marketing literature. From a managerial perspective, businesses should focus on delivering informative, interactive, and trustworthy digital experiences to strengthen consumer trust and enhance purchasing decisions. The study concludes that technological advancements have significantly reshaped how consumers acquire information, build trust, evaluate product alternatives, and make purchasing decisions in a faster, more efficient, and increasingly rational manner.

items.title: Digital involution in AI-assisted academic writing: revisiting educational innovation through empty competition in a postgraduate course
items.abstract: This research note reconsiders the conceptualisation of innovation in the era of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Based on observations from an academic writing course, this research identifies a pattern of excessive textual production with limited intellectual gain. The note interprets this phenomenon as digital involution, in which generative AI lowers the cost of output yet intensifies empty competition among students. The underlying logic aligns with theories of symbolic capital, performativity and algorithmic scale, suggesting that the efficiency of generative AI may increase peer pressure toward quantifiable output at the expense of substantive learning. Rather than defining innovation through productivity and efficiency, this note argues that AI-assisted writing risks a degenerated form of competition through the accelerated production of inflated content and reduced cognitive engagement. The research calls for redesigned assessment and pedagogical practices grounded in the Literacy of Refusal. Future study should prioritise meaningful learning outcomes and the development of critical thinking over textual expansion in AI-assisted environments.

items.title: Digital Pathology and Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Diagnostic Pathology: Implementation, Validation, and Emerging Applications
items.abstract: Digital pathology, driven by whole-slide imaging (WSI), digital slide management, and computational image analysis, is increasingly transforming veterinary diagnostic pathology. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, provides opportunities to automate or assist tasks such as lesion detection, tissue segmentation, mitotic figure identification, immunohistochemistry quantification, and morphometric analysis. However, successful implementation requires more than scanner acquisition or algorithm development. This chapter presents a practice-oriented overview of digital pathology and AI in veterinary diagnostic pathology, emphasizing the complete workflow from tissue processing and slide preparation to scanning, digital viewing, reporting, validation, and quality management. Major pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic sources of error are discussed, together with principles for validating whole-slide imaging for primary diagnosis and maintaining ongoing quality assurance. The chapter also describes major AI task types, annotation and ground-truth challenges, performance evaluation, external validation, model monitoring, and responsible deployment. Particular attention is given to veterinary-specific challenges, including species and breed heterogeneity, stain variability, domain shift, limited annotated datasets, data governance, and automation bias. Emerging approaches such as foundation models, self-supervised learning, multimodal integration, and federated learning are also considered. Overall, effective digital pathology adoption depends on rigorous validation, continuous quality management, appropriate interpretation, and pathologist-led diagnostic accountability. items.title: Digital Transformation in Smart Mobility
items.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified congestion, pollution, and inefficiencies in transportation systems, necessitating sustainable and intelligent mobility solutions. Smart mobility has emerged as a transformative approach driven by digital transformation and advanced technologies. This chapter examines the role of the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Big Data Analytics, and Cloud Computing in enhancing operational efficiency, real-time decision-making, and service integration. It conceptualizes smart mobility through Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS), enabling seamless coordination among stakeholders. Drawing on global and Indian examples, the chapter highlights the impact of digital platforms and electric mobility. It also addresses challenges such as infrastructure limitations, regulatory complexity, data privacy, and the digital divide. Finally, it proposes a framework for sustainable, efficient, and user-centric smart mobility systems.

items.title: Digital Transformation of Insurance Underwriting in Saudi Arabia: Enhancing Risk Selection, Pricing and Operational Efficiency under Vision 2030
items.abstract: Saudi Arabia’s insurance sector is expanding while simultaneously undergoing regulatory, technological and organizational transformation. Under Vision 2030, digital infrastructure, data and artificial intelligence have become explicit enablers of insurance-sector development, creating a strong policy context for redesigning underwriting. This paper examines how digital transformation can improve risk selection, pricing adequacy and operational efficiency in Saudi insurance underwriting while preserving governance, fairness and professional accountability. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize recent peer-reviewed insurance, artificial-intelligence and financial-technology literature with official Saudi policy and market evidence. The analysis identifies five mutually dependent transformation capabilities: integrated and high-quality data, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence, digitally orchestrated workflows, model governance and explainability, and underwriting talent capable of combining actuarial judgment with digital tools. The paper argues that the greatest value does not arise from replacing underwriters, but from redesigning underwriting as a human-in-the-loop decision system in which routine cases can be automated, complex risks are escalated, and pricing decisions are supported by transparent analytics. Saudi market evidence demonstrates rapid premium growth and an increasingly explicit regulatory focus on technology, data and artificial intelligence. However, implementation risks include fragmented data, algorithmic bias, privacy and cybersecurity concerns, legacy-system integration, model drift and inadequate change management. A Saudi Underwriting Digital Transformation Framework is therefore proposed, linking digital foundations, analytics, workflow redesign, governance safeguards and measurable performance outcomes. The framework provides a research and managerial agenda for insurers seeking to improve technical profitability, customer responsiveness and market resilience while aligning digital underwriting with the objectives of Vision 2030.

items.title: Digital Wisdom and GenAI
items.abstract: Within the framework of the European Erasmus+ STIAEM project, the authors of this study deconstruct the assumed homogeneity of “digital natives” regarding generative artificial intelligence adoption. Utilizing a sample of 2,052 secondary school students, the research architecture applies confirmatory factor analysis, extended Bayesian information criterion graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator network analysis, and latent profile analysis. Results identify distinct student profiles based on engagement and familiarity, revealing a profound relational decoupling between technological motivation and situated ethical choices. Under academic deadline pressures, nearly all (92.74%) of the sample participants succumbed to automation bias, uncritically accepting machine hallucinations. This behavioral paradox demonstrates that superficial digital fluency masks severe deficits in epistemic validation and independent thought. Consequently, in this paper the authors argue for shifting from product to process evaluation and integrating explicit algor-ethics interventions within school curricula to develop reflexive, human-centric algorithmic citizenship.

items.title: Discernment in generative AI assisted instructional design: An evaluation map and design heuristics for learning experience designers
items.abstract: Existing research shows that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increases instructional design efficiency. However, there are concerns about pedagogical quality, accuracy and content bias. While prior studies address student passivity in evaluating AI content, the potential for designers to be passive in creating instructional materials remains largely unexplored. This article addresses design safeguards for AI-assisted course and learning-material development through two complementary tools: the Discernment Map, an evaluation checkpoint for instructional designers, and a set of design heuristics. The study is conceptual and design-oriented: both tools were drafted from the literature on AI fluency, automation bias and schema theory, and then refined through structured consultations with six experienced instructional designers in higher education. Though yet to be empirically validated, the practice-informed tools work at two levels: the Map operationalises human oversight of AI outputs across Product, Process and Performance dimensions for each AI-generated artefact, while the heuristics extend discernment into the design of the learning experience itself, so that learners must evaluate rather than accept AI outputs. Both are agile micro-governance tools that integrate critical judgment directly into design workflows. The approach is intended to protect long-term instructional quality against the collective erosion that unchecked AI adoption risks, and to support intentional engagement with AI that reduces automation bias.

items.title: DivAlgo: A systematic evaluation of algorithmic diversity for code generation models
items.abstract: Code generation models are actively being used in professional and educational settings. However, the competence of large language models (LLMs) to generate algorithmically diverse code remains largely unknown. We propose the DivAlgo benchmark, a large-scale dataset constituting algorithmically diverse solutions to programming problems. We also introduce a lightweight similarity metric to enable large-scale evaluation. Our experiments across 24 modern code generation models found that uncontrolled model-generated code is significantly less diverse than human solutions (capturing ~31% of human diversity), and even the best diverse code generation strategy could achieve only ~70% of human diversity. items.title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

items.title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.

items.title: Dynamic engagement patterns during collaborative reasoning discussions and their relations to adolescents’ individual reasoning
items.abstract: Background Collaborative Reasoning (CR) is a dialogic, learner-centered instructional approach shown to promote learners’ higher-order thinking. However, existing research has paid less attention to how learners engage in CR processes and how the temporal dynamics of engagement relate to the development of individual reasoning. Aims To address this gap, this study investigated the temporal development of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement during CR discussions and examined how evolving engagement patterns were associated with subsequent individual reasoning. Sample The participants were 29 seventh-graders from a middle school in China. The students formed four discussion groups, and each group participated in seven CR discussions. Methods The 28 discussions were video-coded for cognitive, emotional, and behavioral interactions (6868 codes). Process mining and epistemic network analysis were used to model shifts in engagement patterns. Individual reasoning was assessed through post-discussion essays. Results Engagement patterns shifted dynamically over time, moving from socially shared regulation to sustained knowledge co-construction. Groups differed in the timing and trajectory of this transition: some groups shifted earlier, whereas others engaged in prolonged regulatory exchanges. The group characterized by later transitions produced fewer basic argumentative elements but more advanced elements in their individual essays. Conclusions This study highlights dynamic engagement patterns as an important link between collaborative processes and learning outcomes and underscores the importance of understanding temporal configurations of regulation and knowledge co-construction in collaborative learning.

items.title: DynamicVis: Dynamic visual perception for efficient remote sensing foundation models
items.abstract: The continuous advancement of remote sensing technology has enabled high-resolution Earth observation; however, interpreting these expansive images using modern Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) remains a significant challenge. Unlike object-centric natural images, remote sensing imagery is fundamentally characterized by extreme target sparsity and massive spatial redundancy. Key objects of interest (e.g., ships, vehicles, scattered buildings) often occupy less than 1% of the spatial extent, surrounded by vast, target-free backgrounds. Many existing VFMs rely on uniform dense processing (e.g., Vision Transformers), while a substantial branch adopts pixel-reconstruction pre-training paradigms (e.g., Masked Autoencoders). These designs may waste substantial computational capacity on modeling redundant backgrounds and dilute the feature representations of small, sparse targets. To bridge this structural misalignment, we propose DynamicVis , a remote sensing visual foundation model explicitly tailored to spatial sparsity in high-resolution imagery, with a focus on large-scale visual pre-training and transferable spatial representations for diverse downstream perception tasks. Architecturally, DynamicVis introduces a Dynamic Region-Aware State Space Model (SSM) that bypasses uniform computation. It adaptively routes and incrementally models only task-relevant, high-salience tokens while employing a parameter-free integration for background context, drastically reducing the complexity of processing ultra-long 2D token sequences ( ∼ 100,000). Crucially, to equip the network with robust spatial-selection capabilities, we propose a novel weakly supervised Region-Level Meta-Embedding Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) pre-training paradigm. Trained on a million-scale dataset, this paradigm promotes foreground-aware regional discrimination in the latent semantic space, mitigating the semantic ambiguity of conventional pixel-reconstruction methods. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse downstream visual perception tasks reveal that DynamicVis achieves competitive performance across region-, instance-, and pixel-level remote sensing tasks, with particularly strong results in sparse-target and instance-level perception tasks (e.g., small object detection and instance segmentation). Notably, DynamicVis processes high-resolution imagery (2048 × 2048) with merely 97 ms latency and 833 MB of memory consumption without employing any acceleration techniques (approximately 6% and 3% of a base ViT, respectively), offering a favorable trade-off between computational scalability and representation accuracy for multi-granular remote sensing analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/KyanChen/DynamicVis .

items.title: Education in the Intelligence Era: Challenges and Reorientation of Contemporary Educational Theories
items.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming contemporary education and challenging established assumptions underlying educational theories. This study aims to examine the challenges posed by AI in the intelligence era and analyze the need for reorientation of contemporary educational theories in response to increasingly complex human–AI interactions. A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted using scholarly literature from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with emphasis on publications from 2019 to 2026. The literature was analyzed through thematic analysis and critical interpretive synthesis, guided by the PRISMA 2020 framework, focusing on knowledge construction, learning processes, assessment, teacher and learner agency, ethics, and educational purposes. The findings indicate that AI is reshaping education through personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated feedback, and expanded knowledge exploration, while simultaneously creating challenges related to knowledge reliability, learner dependency, academic integrity, assessment validity, data privacy, and human agency. The review further shows that constructivism, experiential learning, social learning, connectivism, and humanistic education remain relevant but require critical reorientation to accommodate AI-mediated learning environments. The study proposes a human-centered, AI-augmented educational paradigm that integrates technological intelligence with critical thinking, learner autonomy, teacher agency, ethical reasoning, reflective judgment, and meaningful human interaction.

items.title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
items.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.
